'''Anthony Robert Cashmore''' (born 22 January 1941)<ref name="CV">{{cite web |url=https://live-sas-bio.pantheon.sas.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/2019-10/CV.arc_.pdf |title=Curriculum Vitae, ANTHONY R. CASHMORE |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2019 |website=upenn.edu |publisher= [[University of Pennsylvania]]|access-date=13 Nov 2019 |quote=}}</ref> is a New Zealand [[biochemist]] and plant [[molecular biologist]], best known for identifying [[cryptochrome]] [[photoreceptor protein]]s.<ref name="zz4">{{cite web |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/1998-12/NIoG-IATB-231298.php |title=It's About Time: Biological Clock Research Keeps Ticking|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050521234446/https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/1998-12/NIoG-IATB-231298.php|archive-date=21 May 2005  |author=<!--Not stated--> |date= 23 Dec 1998 |website= eurekalaert.org|publisher=[[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] |access-date= 10 Jan 2020|quote=}}</ref><ref name="HJ2012">{{cite book|author1=Michael F. Holick|author2=Ernst G. Jung|title=Biologic Effects of Light 1998: Proceedings of a Symposium Basel, Switzerland November 1–3, 1998|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=S9YoBgAAQBAJ|accessdate=23 January 2020|date=6 December 2012|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4615-5051-8}}</ref><ref name="PNAS1">{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=C |last2=Yang |first2= H|last3=Guo|first3=H|first4=T|last4=Mockler|last5=Chen|first5=J|last6=Cashmore|first6=AR|date= 1998|title= Enhancement of blue-light sensitivity of Arabidopsis seedlings by a blue light receptor cryptochrome 2 |journal= [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|PNAS]] |volume=95|issue= 5|pages= 2686–2690|doi= 10.1073/pnas.95.5.2686|pmid=9482948 |pmc=19462 |bibcode=1998PNAS...95.2686L |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="hy4">{{cite journal |last1= Ahmad|first1=M |last2= Cashmore|first2= AR|date=1993 |title= HY4 gene of A. thaliana encodes a protein with characteristics of a blue-light photoreceptor|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/366162a0|journal= [[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume= 366|issue= 6451|pages=162–166 |doi= 10.1038/366162a0|pmid=8232555 |bibcode=1993Natur.366..162A |s2cid=4256360 |access-date= 25 Jan 2020|url-access= subscription}}</ref>  These specialized proteins are critical for plant development and play an essential role in [[circadian clock|circadian rhythms]] of plants and animals.<ref name="PNAS1"/><ref name="hy4"/><ref name="Whitelam">{{cite book|author1=Garry C. Whitelam|author2=Karen J. Halliday|title=Annual Plant Reviews, Light and Plant Development|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6hiFESCOPPEC&pg=PA17|accessdate=8 April 2021|date=15 April 2008|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-99429-0|pages=17–}}</ref><ref name="blue">{{cite news |last= Miller|first=Susan Katz |date=20 Nov 1993 |title=Science: Darwin's plants give up their 'blue' secrets|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14019002-700-science-darwins-plants-give-up-their-blue-secrets/ |work= [[New Scientist]]|location= |access-date=8 Apr 2021}}</ref> A [[Professor]] [[Emeritus#In academia|emeritus]] in the Department of Biology at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], Cashmore led the Plant Science Institute from the time of his appointment in 1986 until his retirement in 2011.<ref name="zz1">{{cite web |url=https://live-sas-bio.pantheon.sas.upenn.edu/people/retired-emeritus-faculty |title=Retired/Emeritus Faculty |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2020 |website=Penn Arts & Sciences Department of Biology |publisher=The Trustees of the University of Pennsylvania |access-date=4 Jan 2020 |quote=}}</ref> He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2003.<ref name="NAS2"/>

==Early life and education==
Born in [[Auckland]], New Zealand, in 1941, Cashmore grew up in [[Manawaru]] and [[Te Aroha]]. As a teenager, Cashmore worked in [[Palmerston North]] in the Grasslands Division of [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (New Zealand)|New Zealand's Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR)]].<ref name="PNAS2"/>

Cashmore enrolled at the [[University of Auckland]], majoring in chemistry and completing a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1962, [[Master of Science]] degree in 1963, and [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] degree in 1966.<ref name="CV"/> In 1968 Cashmore moved to [[Cambridge|Cambridge (UK)]] to pursue [[postdoctoral researcher|postdoctoral]] studies at the [[University of Cambridge]] Department of Chemistry, and later at the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology]].<ref name="CV"/><ref name="NAS2"/> In 1971 Cashmore moved to the United States, where he worked as a [[Research Associate]] in the laboratory of [[Michael Chamberlin (biologist)|Michael Chamberlin]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] before returning to New Zealand.<ref name="CV"/><ref name="NAS2"/>

In 1979, Cashmore took a position at the [[Rockefeller University]] (New York), first as a visiting scientist in the laboratory of [[Nam-Hai Chua]], and then as an assistant professor, then Associate Professor.<ref name="tree">{{cite web |url=https://academictree.org/plantbio/peopleinfo.php?pid=817589| title=Plant Biology Tree: Anthony Robert Cashmore |publisher=The Academic Family Tree |date=2021 |access-date=13 Mar 2021}}</ref> In 1986, Cashmore was appointed the Director of the Plant Science Institute at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] ([[Philadelphia]]).<ref name="PNAS1"/><ref name="CV"/> He retired in 2011 and is currently an [[Emeritus]] Professor of Biology at the University of Pennsylvania.<ref name="zz1"/>

==Career==
===Prostratin===
During his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] studies, Cashmore purified the [[toxicity|toxic]] component of ''[[Pimelea prostrata]]'', a New Zealand toxic [[shrub]].<ref name="PNAS2"/> Using [[partition chromatography]], Cashmore purified and [[crystallization|crystallized]] the active component, referred to as [[prostratin]]. Cashmore's studies showed that prostratin was strikingly similar to the [[co-carcinogenic]] [[phorbol esters]] of [[croton oil]], a relationship that was subsequently confirmed using [[chemical synthesis]]<ref name="tetra">{{cite journal |vauthors=CASHMORE AR, SEELYE RN, CAIN BF |title=The structure of prostratin : A toxic tetracyclic diterpene ester from Pimelea Prostrata |date=1976 |url=https://pascal-francis.inist.fr/vibad/index.php?action=getRecordDetail&idt=PASCAL7640295740 |journal= [[Tetrahedron Letters]]|volume=17 |issue= 20|pages=1737–1738 |doi= 10.1016/S0040-4039(00)92940-X|access-date=8 Apr 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[x-ray crystallography]] approaches.<ref name="McCormick">{{cite journal |last1=McCormick |first1=IRN |last2=Nixon|first2=PE|last3=Waters|first3=TN |date= 1976|title=On the structure of prostratin: An X-ray study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0040403900929393 |journal=Tetrahedron Letters |volume=17 |issue=20 |pages=1735–1736 |doi= 10.1016/S0040-4039(00)92939-3|access-date=7 Jul 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Nucleic acid chemistry===
====Hydrazine degradation====
Working with [[George Petersen (biochemist)|George Petersen]] (a New Zealand biochemist) at [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (New Zealand)|New Zealand's Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR)]] (Palmerston North), Cashmore was introduced to the study of [[nucleic acid]]s and how selective chemical reagents could be used to [[DNA sequencing|determine the nucleic acid sequence of DNA]].<ref name="PNAS2">{{cite journal |last1=Nair |first1=Prashant |date= 11 Jan 2011|title=Profile of Anthony R. Cashmore |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=108 |issue=2 |pages=443–5 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.1018069108|pmid=21191100 |pmc=3021040 |bibcode=2011PNAS..108..443N |doi-access=free }}</ref> Cashmore and Petersen examined the use of [[hydrazine]] as a tool to measure [[purine]] nucleotides in samples of [[DNA]].<ref name="hydrazine">{{cite journal |last1=Cashmore |first1=AR |last2= Petersen|first2=GB |date=1969 |title= The degradation of DNA by hydrazine: A critical study of the suitability of the reaction for the quantitative determination of purine nucleotide sequences |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0005278769902895 |journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Nucleic Acids and Protein Synthesis|volume=174 |issue= 2|pages=591–603|doi= 10.1016/0005-2787(69)90289-5|pmid=4888872 |access-date= 28 Jan 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="ax1">{{cite journal |last1=Cashmore |first1=AC |last2= Petersen|first2=GB |date= 1978|title=The degradation of DNA by hydrazine: identification of 3-ureidopyrazole as a product of the hydrazinolysis of deoxycytidylic acid residues |journal= Nucleic Acids Research|volume=5 |issue= 7|pages=2485–2491 |doi= 10.1093/nar/5.7.2485|pmid=353742 |pmc=342178 }}</ref>  Recognizing that hydrazine-treated DNA subsequently exposed to [[alkali]] conditions undergoes degradation, Cashmore defined a quantitative technique for measuring purine nucleotides in DNA samples.<ref name="hydrazine"/> Subsequently, [[Allan Maxam]] and [[Walter Gilbert]] employed the hydrazine degradation approach to develop [[Maxam–Gilbert sequencing]], the first widely adopted method for DNA sequencing.<ref name="MG">{{cite journal |last1=Maxam |first1=AM |author2-link=Walter Gilbert |last2=Gilbert |first2=W |date=1977 |title= A new method for sequencing DNA |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|PNAS]] |volume=74 |issue=2 |pages= 560–564|doi= 10.1073/pnas.74.2.560|pmid=265521 |pmc=392330 |bibcode=1977PNAS...74..560M |doi-access=free |author1-link=Allan Maxam }}</ref>

====tRNA====
Working with Dan Brown<ref name="Brown">{{cite journal |last1=Gait |first1= Michael J. |date=7 Nov 2018 |title=Memoirs: Daniel McGillivray Brown. 3 February 1923—24 April 2012 |journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] |volume= 66|issue= |pages= 79–100|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2018.0008 |s2cid= 81639128 |doi-access=free }}</ref> at [[Cambridge University]], Cashmore demonstrated that the reagent [[methoxyamine]] [[Chemical reaction|reacted]] with a limited number of [[cytosine]] residues in [[Transfer RNA|tRNA]]. Later, Cashmore used the [[Nucleic acid sequence#Sequence determination|RNA sequencing]] procedure that had recently been developed by [[Fred Sanger]] to identify the reactive cytosine residues in a [[tyrosine]] [[epistasis|suppressor]] tRNA of ''[[Escherichia coli]]''.<ref name="1971a">{{cite journal |last1=Cashmore|first1=AR |last2=Brown |first2= DB|last3=Smith|first3=JD|date=1971 |title=Selective reaction of methoxyamine with cytosine bases in tyrosine transfer ribonucleic acid |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0022283671900568 |journal=[[Journal of Molecular Biology]] |volume= 59|issue= 2|pages=359–373 |doi= 10.1016/0022-2836(71)90056-8|pmid=4935788 |access-date=15 Mar 2021|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Studying a mutant of this tRNA, Cashmore identified a new reactive cytosine residue at the base of [[Transfer RNA#Structure|loop III]].<ref name="TC">{{cite journal |last1=Cashmore |first1=T |date=1971 |title= Interaction between Loops I and III in the Tyrosine Suppressor tRNA|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/newbio230236a0 |journal= Nature New Biology|volume=230 |issue= 16|pages= 236–239|doi= 10.1038/newbio230236a0|pmid=5280403 |access-date=10 Jul 2021|url-access=subscription}}</ref> This finding suggested that [[base pair]]ing of conserved residues occurred supporting one of the early models proposed for the three dimensional structure of transfer RNA.<ref name="Levitt">{{cite journal |last1=Levitt |first1=M|date=1969 |title= Detailed molecular model for transfer ribonucleic acid|journal=Nature |volume=224 |issue= 5221|pages=759–763 |doi= 10.1038/224759a0|pmid=5361649|bibcode=1969Natur.224..759L|s2cid=983981}}</ref>

===Biosynthesis of RuBisCO===
[[RuBisCO|Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO)]], thought to be the world's most abundant protein,<ref name="PNAS0">{{cite journal |first1= Yinon |last1=Bar-On|first2=Ron|last2= Milo|date=5 Mar 2019 |title=The global mass and average rate of rubisco |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume=116 |issue= 10|pages=4738–4743 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.1816654116|pmid=30782794|pmc=6410859|doi-access=free|bibcode=2019PNAS..116.4738B }}</ref> utilizes [[photosynthesis|photosynthetic energy]] to [[Biological carbon fixation|fix carbon dioxide]] through the conversion of [[ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate]] to two molecules of [[3-phosphoglycerate]]. It is an [[enzyme]] of interest in the field of [[climate change]] due to its role in [[carbon fixation|fixing carbon dioxide]].<ref name="Dobb">{{cite journal |last1=Dobberstein |first1=B |last2= Blobel|first2=G |last3=Cjua|first3=NH |date=1 Mar 1977 |title= In vitro synthesis and processing of a putative precursor for the small subunit of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase of Chlamydomonas reinhardtii|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume=74 |issue=3 |pages=1082–1085 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.74.3.1082|pmid=265554 |pmc=430598 |bibcode=1977PNAS...74.1082D |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="GW">{{cite web |url=https://economarks.com/will-rubisco-stop-global-warming/ |title= Will Rubisco stop global warming?|last=Cohen |first= Mati|date= 14 December 2019|website=www.economarks.com |publisher=Economarks|access-date=13 Nov 2021 |quote=}}</ref> At New Zealand's DSIR Palmerston North,<ref name="DSIR1">{{cite journal |last1= Cashmore|first1=AR |date=1976 |title=Protein Synthesis in Plant Leaf Tissue: The sites of synthesis of the major proteins |url= http://www.jbc.org/content/251/9/2848.full.pdf|journal=[[Journal of Biological Chemistry]] |volume=251|issue=9 |pages= 2848–2853|doi= 10.1016/S0021-9258(17)33567-6|pmid=1262350 |access-date=19 Jan 2020 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Cashmore studied the biosynthesis of RuBisCO, a multi-[[protein subunit|subunit]] (eight large and eight small subunits) protein located in plant [[chloroplast]]s. Using selective [[protein synthesis inhibitors|inhibitors of protein synthesis]] Cashmore showed that in contrast to the RuBisCO large subunit (which was known to be synthesized on chloroplast ribosomes), the small subunit of RuBisCO was produced as a soluble [[protein precursor|precursor protein]] on [[cytoplasm]]ic [[ribosome]]s.<ref name="gray">{{cite journal |last3=Gray |first3=RE |last1=Cashmore |first1=A|last2=Broadhurst|first2=K |date=1978 |title=Cell-free synthesis of leaf protein: Identification of an apparent precursor of the small subunit of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase |url=https://www.pnas.org/content/pnas/75/2/655.full.pdf |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]] |volume=108 |issue= 2|pages=595–608 |doi= 10.1073/pnas.75.2.655|pmid=16592495 |pmc=411314 |bibcode=1978PNAS...75..655C |access-date=21 Jul 2021|doi-access=free }}</ref> The soluble precursor protein is subsequently processed and imported into chloroplasts.<ref name="Highfield">{{cite journal |last1=Highfield |first1=PE |last2=Ellis |first2=RJ |date=2 Feb 1978 |title=Synthesis and transport of the small subunit of chloroplast ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/271420a0|journal=Nature |volume=271 |issue= 5644|pages=420–424 |doi= 10.1038/271420a0|bibcode=1978Natur.271..420H |s2cid=4188202 |access-date=28 Nov 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Lubben">{{cite journal |last1=Lubben |first1=TH |last2=Theg |first2=SM|last3=Keegstra|first3=K |date= 1988|title= Transport of proteins into chloroplasts|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00047688 |journal=Photosynthesis Research |volume= 17|issue= 1–2|pages=173–194 |doi= 10.1007/BF00047688|pmid=24429668 |bibcode=1988PhoRe..17..173L |s2cid=922287 |access-date=28 Nov 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Light-regulated enhancer sequences===
At [[Rockefeller University]], Cashmore studied [[Nucleic acid sequence|DNA sequences]] associated with light regulated [[gene expression|expression]] of a [[pea]] nuclear RuBisCO small subunit gene.<ref name="Estrella">{{cite journal |last1=Herrera-Estrella |first1=L |last2= Van den Broeck|first2=G|last3=Van Montagu |first3=M|last4=Schell|first4=J|last5=Timko|first5=M|last6=Cashmore|first6=A |date=1984 |title=Light-inducible and chloroplast-associated expression of a chimaeric gene introduced into Nicotiana tabacum using a Ti plasmid vector |journal= Nature|volume=310 |issue= 5973|pages=115–120 |doi= 10.1038/310115a0|pmid=6330570 |bibcode=1984Natur.310..115H |s2cid=4307727 }}</ref> For these studies, Cashmore collaborated with scientists in the laboratory of [[Jozef Schell|Jeff Schell]] and [[Marc Van Montagu]] in [[Ghent]] (Belgium).<ref name="Estrella2">{{cite journal |last1=Estrella |first1=Luis |title= My journey into the birth of plant transgenesis and its impact on modern plant biology|journal= Biography of Pioneers in Plant Biotechnology|year=2020 |volume= 18|issue= 7|pages= 1487–1491|doi= 10.1111/pbi.13319|doi-access=free |pmid=31883186 |pmc=7292536 |bibcode=2020PBioJ..18.1487H }}</ref> Using [[transgene|transgenic]] plant cells, they demonstrated that in the pea plant, light-regulated [[gene expression|expression]] was mediated by a 1 kilobase (kb) [[promoter (genetics)|promoter]] fragment.<ref name="Estrella"/> In a second study, this DNA fragment was shown to have the properties of an [[Enhancer (genetics)|enhancer sequence]], functioning in either orientation and when fused to a normally non-light-regulated promoter.<ref name="Timko">{{cite journal |last1=Timko |first1=M |last2=Kausch|first2=A|last3=Castresana|first3=C|last4=Fassler|first4=J|last5=Herrera-Estrella|first5=L|last6=Van den Broeck|first6=G|last7=Van Montagu|first7=M|last8=Schell|first8=J|last9=Cashmore|first9=A|date= 1985|title=Light regulation of plant gene expression by an upstream enhancer-like element |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/318579a0 |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume=318 |issue= 6046|pages= 579–582|doi= 10.1038/318579a0|pmid=3865055 |bibcode=1985Natur.318..579T |s2cid=4307881 |access-date=15 Dec 2019 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

===Cryptochrome===
In 1881, [[Francis Darwin]] and [[Charles Darwin]] demonstrated that plants exhibited a [[phototropism|phototropic response]] to blue light.<ref name="Sci">{{cite magazine |last=Miller |first=Susan Katz |date=20 Nov 1993 |title= Science: Darwin's plants give up their 'blue' secrets |url= https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg14019002-700-science-darwins-plants-give-up-their-blue-secrets/ |magazine=[[New Scientist]] |location= |publisher= |access-date=8 Dec 2019 }}</ref><ref name="Briggs">{{cite journal |last1= Briggs|first1=Winslow  |date= 1993|title=New light on stem growth |url= https://www.nature.com/articles/366110a0.pdf |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |volume= 366|issue= 6451|pages=110–111 |doi= 10.1038/366110a0|pmid=8232548 |bibcode=1993Natur.366..110B |s2cid=42260720 |access-date=5 Jan 2020 }}</ref><ref name="Darwin_1881">{{cite book | last = Darwin | first = Charles | title = The Power of Movement in Plants | url = https://archive.org/details/powermovementin06darwgoog | year = 1881 | publisher = D. Appleton and Company | location = New York}}</ref> Elusive to discovery, scientists gave the name [[cryptochrome]] to the [[photoreceptor protein|photoreceptor]] factor(s) responsible for this effect.<ref name="Gressel">{{cite journal|last1=Gressel|first1= J|date=1979|title=Blue Light Photoreception|journal=Photochemistry and Photobiology|volume=30|issue=6|pages= 749–754|doi= 10.1111/j.1751-1097.1979.tb07209.x|bibcode= 1979PcPb...30..749G|s2cid= 98643540|access-date=28 Nov 2021|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1751-1097.1979.tb07209.x|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Interested in adopting the "power of ''[[Arabidopsis]]'' genetics" for the study of light regulation,<ref name="blue"/> in 1980 Cashmore, working with post-doctoral student Margaret Ahmad, identified ''Arabidopsis'' [[mutant]]s that showed reduced sensitivity to blue light. Using [[DNA sequencing]] and [[complementation (genetics)|complementation]] techniques, Cashmore and Ahmed [[Molecular cloning|cloned]] the gene and discovered that the mutants were [[allele]]s of a previously identified ''hy4'' mutant.<ref name="hy4"/> Ahmad and Cashmore called this blue light photoreceptor "cryptochrome", and it is now referred to as CRY1.<ref name="hy4"/><ref name="CRY1">{{cite journal |last1=Lin |first1= C|last2=Robertson |first2=D|last3=Raibekas| first3=A|last4=Jorns|first4=M|last5=Dutton|first5=P|last6=Cashmore|first6=A |date= 1995|title=Association of flavin adenine dinucleotide with the Arabidopsis blue light receptor CRY1 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.7638620?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%20%200pubmed |journal=Science |volume=269 |issue= 5226|pages=968–970|doi= 10.1126/science.7638620|pmid= 7638620|bibcode= 1995Sci...269..968L|s2cid= 40649563|access-date=30 Dec 2021|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Cashmore's research group identified a second member of the cryptochrome family (CRY2) using [[cDNA library]] screening.<ref name="PNAS1"/> This research was the foundation that led to the identification of CRY proteins in other plant species, bacteria, fungi, animals, and humans, as well as research that defined the pivotal role of these proteins in [[circadian clock]] regulation across species<ref name="blue"/><ref name="nobel">{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2017/advanced-information/ |title= Scientific Background Discoveries of Molecular Mechanisms Controlling the Circadian Rhythm|last1=Hall |first1= Jeffrey|last2=Rosbach|first2=Michael|last3=Young|first3=Michael|date= 2017|website=nobelprize.org |publisher=Nobel Prize Outreach |access-date= 10 Dec 2021|quote=}}</ref> and as the primary sensory molecule enabling light-dependent [[magnetoreception|magnetic compass orientation]] in migratory birds.<ref name="bird">{{cite journal |last1=Einwich |first1= Angelika|last2=Dedek |first2= Karin|last3=Seth|first3=Pranav Kumar|last4=Laubinger|first4=Sascha|last5=Mouritsen|first5=Henrik|date= 25 Sep 2020|title= A novel isoform of cryptochrome 4 (Cry4b) is expressed in the retina of a night-migratory songbird |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=10 |issue= 1|pages=15794 |doi= 10.1038/s41598-020-72579-2 |doi-access= free|pmid= 32978454|pmc= 7519125|bibcode= 2020NatSR..1015794E}}</ref> Today, light-based diagnostic and therapeutic [[Wearable technology|wearable]] photonic healthcare devices, are based on the function of the cryptochrome photoreceptors.<ref name="tech">{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=G-H |last2=Moon |first2=H|last3=Kim|first3=H|last4=Lee|first4=GH|last5=Kwon|first5=W|last6=Yoo|first6=S|last7=Myung|first7=D|last8=Yun|first8=SH|last9=Bao|first9=Z|last10=Hahn|first10=SK |date=2020 |title=Multifunctional materials for implantable and wearable photonic healthcare devices |journal= Nature Reviews Materials|volume= 5|issue= 2|pages= 149–165|doi=10.1038/s41578-019-0167-3 |pmid=32728478 |pmc=7388681 |bibcode=2020NatRM...5..149L }}</ref>

===Human behavior, free will and consciousness===
In recent years, Cashmore turned his attention to the topic of human behavior, studying the concepts of [[free will]] and [[consciousness]]. In a publication on this topic,<ref name="Luc">{{cite journal |last=Cashmore |first=AR |date= 2010|title=The Lucretian swerve: The biological basis of human behavior and the criminal justice system |journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|PNAS]] |volume=107|issue=10|pages= 4499–4504|doi= 10.1073/pnas.0915161107|pmid=20142481 |pmc=2842067 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Cashmore noted that in popular discussions regarding the relative importance of [[nature vs nurture]], an element that is commonly missing is awareness that individuals are responsible for neither their genetic inheritance nor their environment.<ref name="Luc"/> Based on this observation, he therefore asked "where does this notion of free will come from?" and challenged the [[scientific community]] to reconsider the concept of free will.<ref name="Luc"/>

Applying the [[scientific method]] to probe the concept from a [[Philosophy of Information]] approach, Cashmore argued that all [[biological systems]] – including humans – obey the laws of chemistry and physics. Cashmore further suggested that the concept of free will '' "is an illusion, akin to religious beliefs or the outdated belief in [[vitalism]]''", equivalent to the continuing belief in [[Cartesian duality]], and therefore contradictory to society's interpretation of [[accountability]] in the [[criminal justice]] system.<ref name="Luc"/><ref name="Caruso">{{cite book|author=Gregg D. Caruso|title=Exploring the Illusion of Free Will and Moral Responsibility|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Vmu0lkE6J-IC&pg=PA186|accessdate=28 January 2020|date=5 July 2013|publisher=Lexington Books|isbn=978-0-7391-7732-7|pages=186–}}</ref> The article stimulated discussion and analysis by scientists in the fields of [[biology]], [[behavioral sciences]], and [[philosophy]].<ref name="Radoilska2012">{{cite book|author=Lubomira Radoilska|title=Autonomy and Mental Disorder|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HVo6ORK-Y-sC&pg=PA33|accessdate=28 January 2020|date=19 April 2012|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=978-0-19-959542-6|pages=33–}}</ref> Scientist and author [[Jerry Coyne]] stated that after reading this article on [[determinism]] and the criminal justice system, he was ‘instantly converted to determinism’.<ref name="maroon">{{cite news |last=Harris|first=Lee |date=2018|title= Meet Jerry Coyne, the University's Most Prolific and Provocative Emeritus Blogger|url=https://www.chicagomaroon.com/article/2018/2/15/meet-jerry-coyne-universitys-prolific-provocative/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181116050934/https://www.chicagomaroon.com/article/2018/2/15/meet-jerry-coyne-universitys-prolific-provocative/|archive-date=16 November 2018|work=[[The Chicago Maroon]] |location= Chicago, USA|access-date=30 Dec 2019 }}</ref><ref name="Mele2014">{{cite book|author=Alfred R. Mele|title=Free: Why Science Hasn't Disproved Free Will| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nAJ_BAAAQBAJ&pg=PT53|accessdate=5 Jan 2020|date=2 September 2014|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-937164-8|pages=53–}}</ref><ref name="phys">{{cite web |url=https://phys.org/news/2010-03-free-illusion-biologist.html |title=Free will is an illusion, biologist says |last= Zyga|first=Lisa |date=2010 |website= phys.org|publisher= Science X|access-date=20 Dec 2019 |quote=}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Cashmore was a Professor of Biology at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] and Director of the Plant Science Institute there until his retirement in 2011.<ref name="NAS2"/> Since 2011, he has been a Professor emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania (Department of Biology).<ref name="NAS2"/> Cashmore has authored more than 100 refereed research papers and has served on the editorial boards of the publications Plant Molecular Biology, [[The Plant Journal]], and the [[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America]].<ref name="NAS2"/><ref name="edit">{{cite web |url= https://nrc88.nas.edu/pnas_search/memberDetails.aspx?ctID=20002156|title= About the PNAS Member Editor: Anthony Cashmore|author=<!--Not stated--> |date= 2021|website= [[National Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=22 Dec 2021 |quote=}}</ref> He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2003.<ref name="NAS2">{{cite web |url=https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/plant-biologist-anthony-cashmore-elected-national-academy-sciences |title=Plant Biologist Anthony Cashmore Elected to National Academy of Sciences |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=5 May 2003 |website=penntoday.upenn.edu |publisher=University of Pennsylvania |access-date=13 Nov 2019 |quote=}}</ref><ref name="NAS1">{{cite web |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/anthony-r-cashmore-0cz1hg/ |title=Member Directory: Anthony Cashmore|author=<!--Not stated-->|date=2021|website=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |access-date=8 Apr 2021 |quote=}}https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/anthony-r-cashmore-0cz1hg/</ref>

==Personal life==
Cashmore was born in [[Auckland]] ([[New Zealand]]), to parents Nancy and Norman Cashmore.<ref name="birth">{{cite web |url=https://en.geneanet.org/fonds/bibliotheque/?go=1&lang=en&language__en__=en&nom=cashmore&page=1&size=50 |title=Town Topics |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2019 |website=geneanet.org |publisher=Geneanet |access-date=13 Nov 2019 |quote=}}</ref> He is married to American [[Neuroscientist]] and [[Geneticist]] [[Nancy Bonini]].<ref name="spouse">{{cite news |last=Kelly|first=Morgan|title=Geoscientist William Bonini, dedicated teacher and genial colleague, dies at 90 |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2017/01/03/geoscientist-william-bonini-dedicated-teacher-and-genial-colleague-dies-90 |work= [[Princeton University]] News|location=Princeton, NJ, USA |date=3 Jan 2017 |access-date= 12 Jul 2019}}</ref>
